title: Justice like a torrent (Amos 5:21–24)
hook: God doesn't want songs without justice for the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea and Gomer: after all the anger, therefore, tenderness. Your line was speak to her heart. Today the week ends.

In August 1963, on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, Martin Luther King Jr. reached for the words of a shepherd from the eighth century before Christ. His name was Amos. He said himself he wasn't a prophet or a prophet's son; he was a herdsman who tended fig trees, from a small town called Tekoa in the south. God sent him north, to Bethel, the royal shrine of the kingdom of Israel, in a time of money and peace. The festivals were full, the music magnificent. And Amos stood up in the middle of it with a message nobody wanted.
screen: `1963, THE LINCOLN MEMORIAL.` → `A HERDSMAN FROM TEKOA.` → `FULL FESTIVALS AT BETHEL.`

segments.voice: Amos speaks in God's voice, and it's blunt. I hate your feast days. I won't accept your offerings. Take away the noise of your songs; I won't listen to the music of your harps. But read the chapters around it. Amos has just described people who sell the poor for a pair of shoes, who trample the heads of the needy into the dust, who take bribes at the town gate where justice was meant to be done. The problem isn't singing. It's singing at the festival and cheating at the market the next morning. Then the line King quoted, in the Douay-Rheims: "judgment shall be revealed as water, and justice as a mighty torrent." The Hebrew picture is exact. Most streams in that land are wadis, dry gullies that roar after a storm and are empty by summer. Amos asks for a nachal eitan, a stream that never fails. Not justice that flares up when a cause trends and is gone in a month. Justice that runs all year. Catholic social teaching speaks of a preferential option for the poor, and this is one of its roots. Look back at the week: a boy known before he was formed, a potter remaking clay, a covenant written on the heart, mercies new every morning, bones that breathe, a husband who speaks tenderly, and a stream that doesn't dry up. Seven pictures of a God who keeps coming back, and wants his people to keep coming back to the poor.
screen: `TAKE AWAY THE NOISE OF YOUR SONGS.` · `THE POOR SOLD FOR A PAIR OF SHOES.` · `NOT A WADI: A STREAM THAT NEVER FAILS.` · `A WEEK OF PROPHETS, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `JUSTICE AS A MIGHTY TORRENT.`

segments.voice: Let a prayer, hymn or song you love play in your head for a moment. Then think of one person near you who is treated unfairly, or poor and overlooked, and of one concrete thing, a fair word, a shared meal, a bill paid on time, that would let a little justice flow their way. If you pray, offer the song and the person together.
nachal eitan. Hebrew for an ever-flowing stream: Amos's demand that justice for the poor run like that, never drying up. Today's word.
Your line: justice that runs all year. A stream, not a wadi. Day four hundred twenty-seven, and the week, done.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes join worship with works of justice and mercy, and Catholic social teaching, drawing on prophets like Amos, speaks of a preferential option for the poor.

chat.says: Why would Amos say God hates their feasts and songs?
options: Not the singing itself: they sang at feasts, then cheated the poor at market.
God dislikes music in worship, so Amos told them to pray in silence.
The festivals had grown too long, so Amos wanted shorter services.
chat.meaning: The problem isn't singing. It's worship alongside selling the poor for a pair of shoes. God asks for justice like a stream that never fails.

Tekoa.meaning: Amos's small hometown in the south

Bethel.meaning: the royal shrine of the northern kingdom of Israel

wadis.meaning: dry gullies that roar after a storm, empty by summer

preferential option for the poor.meaning: Catholic social teaching: the poor come first in our concern
